theme: A morning out is a sequence: first, then, next

activities.title: Put the morning in order
activities.intro: A morning out is a story, and stories have an order. I will say some things that happen on a morning you go out, all mixed up. Put them in the order they really happen, first, then, next.
activities.offScreen: Go and tell a grown up the three things you do first every single morning, in order, without missing any out.

rounds.prompt: Two things from a morning out. Putting your shoes on, and waking up. Put them in the order they happen.
Three things. Putting your bag on, waking up, and eating breakfast. Put them in the order they happen.
Three more. Walking to the library, putting your bag in the basket, and putting your shoes on. Put them in the order they happen.

items.sound: putting your bag in the basket

rounds.prompt: The whole morning, four things. Eating breakfast, waking up, putting your bag on, and getting dressed. Put them in order.

activities.title: What do you need for this bit of the day
activities.intro: Every part of the day needs a different thing. I will tell you which part of the day it is, and you tap the thing you would need.
activities.offScreen: Go and find one thing in your house you would need for a morning out, carry it to a grown up, and tell them what part of the day it is for.

rounds.prompt: It is time for a drink of water. Tap the one you need.
It is snack time and you are hungry. Tap the one you can eat.
It is drawing time. Tap the one you draw with.
It is time to go home and you have to carry all your things. Tap the one you carry them in.

activities.title: Counting what goes in the bag
activities.intro: Time to pack. I will show you what is going in the bag, and you count it and tell me how many. Point at each one as you count, so none of them get counted twice.
activities.offScreen: Go and pack a real bag with a grown up, and count out loud every single thing as it goes in.

rounds.prompt: Here are the pencils going into the bag, in two little piles. Count all the pencils. How many?
Your friends are waiting at the table, over at the side. They are not going in the bag. Count the books in the pile. How many books?
Here are the crayons for the pencil case, in two piles. Count all the crayons. How many?
Your friends are at the side again, waiting. Do not count them. Count the apples in the pile. How many apples?

parentCard.title: The four picture morning strip, cut up and rebuilt
steps: Fold a sheet of paper into four boxes and hand them the pencil. Ask them what happens first on a morning out and let them draw it in the first box, however it comes out. You do not draw, you do not tidy it, and you do not say what it should look like.

Fill the other three boxes the same way, one thing per box, and let them say out loud what each picture is as they finish it. If they want five things and there are four boxes, let them solve that themselves.

Cut the strip apart together, one box at a time, then shuffle the four pieces face up on the table. Let them rebuild the order, saying first, then, next and last out loud as they lay each one down. Shuffle and do it again, and see whether the second go is faster.
Now pack a real bag for a morning out in that same order, with the real things, and let them do the zips and the buckles even when it takes a while.

Finish with the strong voice. They pick a question they might want to ask somebody at the library, stand up, and ask it loudly enough for somebody in the next room to hear. Then ask it back to them in a tiny mouse voice so they can hear the difference, and let them laugh at you.
notice: Do they lay the pieces down first and then tell the story, or do they tell the story out loud and let their hands follow it?
On the second shuffle, do they rebuild it faster, or do they treat it as a brand new puzzle every time?
When they use the strong voice, does anything else change with it, their back or their chin or where they are looking, or is it only the volume?
